t: Finding MK Average — Order Statistics on a Sliding Window
o:
**Understanding the problem**

We continuously track the last m stream elements. calculateMKAverage returns -1 until m elements exist; afterwards it throws away the k smallest and the k largest of the window and floors the average of the remaining m - 2k values. Tracing the sample (m = 3, k = 1): after adding 3 and 1 the window is incomplete, so -1. Adding 10 fills it: window {1, 3, 10}, discard 1 and 10, average of {3} is 3. Later additions slide the window: {10, 5, 5} averages to 5, then {5, 5, 5} to 5. With up to 10^5 calls and m up to 10^5, re-sorting the window per query is far too slow; we need incremental order statistics with prefix sums.
k: Each addElement inserts one value and (once full) evicts exactly one — update a sorted structure incrementally instead of re-sorting.
Dropping the k extremes needs only two prefix quantities over sorted values: sums of the k smallest and of the (m - k) smallest; their difference is the middle sum.
Values are bounded by 10^5, so a Fenwick tree indexed by value supplies counts, sums and kth-element walks in O(log V).

a.n: Approach 1: Re-sort the Window on Demand
a.i: Keep the live window in a deque. On each calculateMKAverage, copy and sort it, slice off k elements from both ends, and average the middle. Trivially correct — the perfect baseline to cite before optimizing; sorting the entire window per query is exactly what kills it at scale.
s: Deque stores the last m elements; popleft whenever it exceeds m.
calculateMKAverage: return -1 if fewer than m elements are stored.
Sort a copy of the window; sum positions k through m - k - 1.
a.t: O(m log m) per calculation while addElement is O(1); around ten billion steps at the constraint limits, so it TLEs

a.n: Approach 2: Fenwick Tree over the Value Range
a.i: Index a Fenwick tree by value (1..10^5) keeping two parallel arrays — occurrence counts and value sums — alongside a deque holding the window for eviction. Inserts and deletes each toggle one tree path. The sum of the k smallest values comes from a bit-descent that finds the k-th smallest value v: take the prefix sum up to v, then subtract the surplus duplicates (prefixCount(v) - k) * v. With lo = sum of the k smallest and hi = sum of the (m - k) smallest, the middle sum is exactly hi - lo, and the answer is (hi - lo) divided by (m - 2k), floored.
s: addElement(num): append to the deque and BIT-add (+1, +num); if the deque now exceeds m, BIT-add (-1, -front) and popleft.
sumOfKSmallest(k): descend the tree power by power to locate the largest prefix whose count is below k; v is that position plus 1.
Return prefixSum(v) minus (prefixCount(v) - k) copies of v to trim ties at the boundary value.
calculateMKAverage: return -1 below m elements; otherwise floor((sumOfKSmallest(m - k) - sumOfKSmallest(k)) / (m - 2k)).
a.t: O(log V) per addElement and two O(log V) walks per calculation (V = 10^5) — comfortably fits 10^5 operations
a.sp: O(V) for the two Fenwick arrays plus O(m) for the eviction deque

w:
**Wrap-up**

Cite the brute force first, then justify the Fenwick design from the operation budget. Pitfalls: forgetting eviction once the deque overflows, off-by-one in the kth descent (largest prefix with count below k; answer is position + 1), trimming surplus duplicates when the boundary value repeats, and using 32-bit sums (window totals reach 10^10). The classic alternative is three ordered multisets (smallest-k, middle, largest-k buckets with running sums and rebalancing on insert/evict); it matches O(log n) but is fiddlier to implement. Follow-ups: arbitrary deletions or median queries reuse the same tree unchanged.
